Analysis by Annabel Crabb

When it comes to budget coverage, debt and deficits usually dominate the headlines.

But budgets, and fiscal policy in general, are far more than a mere book-balancing exercise.

We want to know what issues matter to this federal budget. Have your say.

They also incorporate powerful tools that redistribute wealth and income within society, usually via the tax system.

Australia has long been a country with a "progressive" tax system where those on higher incomes pay a higher proportion of their pay in taxes.

As a result, they usually pay a great deal more.

For most of the past quarter century, however, the pendulum has swung back towards workers rather than those who earn a buck from investment.

On top of lucrative superannuation incentives, which delivered higher income groups much bigger tax discounts on contributions and tax-free income upon retirement, property investment became a beacon for those looking to build wealth.

But it was negative gearing, which allows investors to deduct losses from rental properties from their salaries, combined with a heavily discounted capital gains tax bill on profits from the sale of investment properties that has most enraged the youth.

Real estate has quadrupled in value over the past 25 years, well above the growth in wages.

The lurks have also cost the nation dearly.

According to a 2024 Treasury study, negative gearing was expected to cost the budget $7.7 billion this financial year in foregone revenue. Added to the expected $5.87 billion in lost revenue on the capital gains tax discount, that's a total of $13.57 billion.

The benefits of those foregone cash receipts overwhelmingly accrue to the nation's highest income earners.

The end result? Australia is home to some of the highest-priced real estate on the planet.

Handing out tax incentives is easy. Clawing them back is not.

The changes already have been erroneously described as tax hikes rather than the curtailing of tax benefits.

According to the budget statements, the changes to both negative gearing and capital gains tax will pull in just $1.35 billion in the first year and $2.3 billion in the second.

That's a long way short of the cash Treasury reckons is lost on the tax incentives, mostly explained by the decision to grandfather the changes.

Those with existing investment properties will continue to reap the gains of negative gearing, while the original capital gains tax arrangements will also remain in place until a hybrid system kicks into place after the changes are introduced next year.

Without the grandfathering, the political backlash would have been more severe, given the 1.2 million negatively geared property households.

It also would have had the potential to send property prices into a sharp decline.

While most first home buyers would welcome a sharp drop, it could have caused some issues with a real estate-obsessed banking system.

The mooted changes are likely to have only a modest impact in the early years and gradually increase as older investors sell.

Topic: Stock Market

Several tax measures to help small business with cash flow have been made permanent in the budget. ( ABC News: John Gunn )

The federal budget suggests that changes to capital gains tax could see investment shift from property to shares.

The current flat 50pc CGT discount will be replaced with indexation aligned with inflation, with a minimum tax rate of 30pc applying to real capital gains accruing from next July.

The government has introduced measures to lessen the tax burden on smaller businesses, including making the instant asset write-off and loss carry back permanent.

Investors in the share market are undercompensated for the impact of inflation under current capital gains tax (CGT) settings, according to the budget.

As expected, the federal government will scrap the flat 50 per cent CGT discount for investments for more than 12 months, a measure largely sold as addressing intergenerational housing inequality.

But the budget also highlighted the potential to shift investment away from existing properties and into stocks and new properties.

"The reforms to negative gearing and capital gains tax are expected to improve the efficiency of investment decisions, as they are more likely to be made for economic reasons rather than tax outcomes," the budget read.

Federal budget 2026 : Look back at how the day's events unfolded with our blog.

Stock investors had raised concerns about CGT changes ahead of the budget, including younger Australians who had invested in shares instead of property due to being locked out of the housing market.

Established private investor Liam Walsh holds $3 million of high-growth shares, chasing capital gains.

"I'm looking for some tissues to cry into because nearly all of my income that I derive comes from capital growth," he told The Business.

Liam Walsh supports CGT changes despite expecting to take a financial hit. ( ABC News: Adam Wyatt )

Despite expecting to take a personal hit on the reform, Mr Walsh supports the policy.

Broadly, however, data in the budget showed that investors in the Australian share market have been undercompensated for the impact of inflation by the current CGT settings.

The CGT discount does not appropriately compensate investors in the share market, according to the budget. ( Supplied: Treasury, ASX, ABS )

For example, inflation made up 56 per cent of asset price growth for ASX 200 shares held for 10 years to March 2026.

For the broader All Ordinaries index, inflation accounted for 53 per cent of growth.

Over the same period, inflation accounted for 38 per cent of asset price growth for all property, meaning the flat 50 per cent discount would overcompensate for inflation.

Devika Shivadekar, an economist at consultancy firm RSM Australia, said the CGT changes would likely incentivise people to think about other methods of wealth building outside of property.

"Australians' obsession with building property portfolios has, over time, created an inequity between the haves and the hopefuls," Ms Shivadekar said.

"In isolation, CGT changes might cost share investors, but it will likely encourage people to look for investments outside of property."

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the current system was encouraging investors to "pile into existing housing, pushing prices up, and blocking people out of the housing market, particularly younger people".

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson said the opposition would not be supporting the changes to negative gearing or the CGT discount.

Jacki Neumann, the head of capital markets at investment app Sharesies, described the changes as signalling "a structural transition in how Australians are incentivised to build wealth".

"By moving the needle from tax advantages towards market-driven returns, the focus for the everyday investor shifts from navigating tax structures to evaluating the fundamental quality of their investments," Ms Neumann said ahead of the budget.

The government is aiming to move investors towards new property and shares. ( AAP: Lukas Coch )

However, the changes will "change the equation" for growth investors, she added.

"While a move toward an indexation framework aims for a more equitable environment, it creates a threshold where the tax benefits of indexation diminish once an asset's growth significantly outpaces inflation.

UBS equity strategist Richard Schellbach agreed that the CGT changes, combined with the winding back of negative gearing, could see stocks "improve their relative appeal" compared to property investments.

In a note to clients ahead of the budget, he said that would increase the relative appeal of income stocks, which pay a reliable dividend, over growth stocks.

Analysis by Ian Verrender

In the lead-up to budget night, some high-profile investors had argued that scrapping the 50 per cent CGT discount could hurt startups , which often use employee share schemes.

Startups utilise share schemes to attract talent, offering a potentially lucrative payday should the company succeed, making up for their inability to match the bigger salaries of more established competitors.

Employees would then be liable to pay tax on any capital gains made if they sold their shares.

The budget acknowledged "the unique characteristics of the tech and startup sector" and flagged a period of consultation ahead.

The government has also introduced measures to lessen the tax burden on smaller businesses, as they face inflationary pressures from the Iran war fallout.

The ability of businesses with turnovers up to $10 million to instantly write off assets up to $20,000 will be made permanent, giving firms certainty rather than waiting for yearly extensions.

For example, a restaurant investing $18,000 in a new deep fryer and $2,000 on new furniture can immediately reduce its taxable profit by $20,000, rather than having to claim those assets over several years.

Small businesses can continue to claim refunds for tax losses against previously profitable years. ( Supplied: rawpixel.com )

The government estimated it will save small businesses around $32 million in compliance costs each year.

"We're making tax time simple for small businesses, which will save them 376,000 hours a year," Mr Chalmers said.

The budget also contained reforms aimed at improving cash flow for small-to-medium businesses.

"It helps with cash flow when you need it most. A business having a rough year doesn't just need sympathy, it needs actual cash," Ms Shivadekar said.

Mr Chalmers said that change is aimed at "bolstering resilience and risk-taking".

Around 85,000 companies will now be able to "carry back" losses from the current tax year to obtain a refund of taxes paid on profits in the previous two years.

The government said the permanent scheme would benefit mostly small businesses, with companies turning over up to $1 billion a year eligible for refunds.

"It's the norm in most developed countries."

It will cost $890 million to deliver over the next five years.

Josh Ball, the co-founder of produce subscription service Farmers Pick, welcomed the loss carry back being made permanent.

"With business there's a whole set of risks that we play into, and being able to have that somewhat de-risked or be able to have that flexibility, really enables businesses to sustain challenging periods such as shocks with fuel and fertiliser," he told The Business.

The government will consult the startup sector on the impact of CGT reforms. ( Unsplash: Annie Spratt )

So that startups, which are unlikely to have turned a profit yet, do not miss out, an additional budget measure will allow businesses to claim refunds for tax losses in their first two years of operation.

Coming in from July 2028, the so-called loss refundability measure will be capped at the amount a startup has paid in fringe benefits tax and withholding tax paid on employee wages.

The government said the business tax reforms in the budget were "expected to support investment, innovation, risk-taking and resilience".

By Annabel Crabb

Topic: Budget

The language of generational change is everywhere in this budget. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts )

In all likelihood, Anthony Norman Albanese will be this country's last baby boomer prime minister.

But he has now officially donned the cape of Youth Warrior, addressing himself to the unwinding of policies that for decades have plumped his own generation's asset sheets with tidy two-bedders, sure-fire flippers and solid family homes (close all facs, public transport).

This moment has been coming for some time, as home ownership rates ebbed among the young and swelled among the old, and as the massed ranks of millennials and gen Zs eligible to vote gradually approached and then outnumbered baby boomers.

Federal budget 2026 : Look back at how the day's events unfolded with our blog.

The prime minister was born into exceedingly modest circumstances, but like many in his cohort, he caught a few breaks over his lifetime.

He received a free university education and caught the Sydney real estate wave at the right time. Of the 226 present serving members of the parliament, he's one of a handful who've been around long enough to be on the "old" parliamentary super scheme, guaranteeing a handsome income for life.

And tonight he becomes the first serving prime minister in decades to take a hammer to the most sacred shibboleth in Australian domestic politics: the assumption that housing in Australia is not just a life essential fairly high on Maslow's hierarchy of needs, but also an investment opportunity that presents, to the shrewd operator, a lower-taxed path to wealth than the orthodox technique of having a job.

In all likelihood, Anthony Norman Albanese will be this country's last baby boomer prime minister. ( Facebook: University of Sydney )

The buzzword across the 2026 budget and the introductory speech delivered by the treasurer is "ambitious". And it is indeed an ambitious thing for a government to shut down tax breaks that have earned a great many people a great deal of wealth.

What's steeled the prime minister, apart from his impatient treasurer, is the growing sentiment among younger generations (who are also the voters with the most elections in their future) that they are getting the rubber end of the real estate plunger. That they are priced out of the real estate market, obliged to pay ludicrously high rents to landlords who, thanks to a heady admixture of advantageous tax settings and timing, are sometimes holding multiple properties.

The language of generational change is everywhere in this budget. Private health insurance concessions for the over 65s are to be whipper-snipped to the tune of $3 billion. A wholesale redraw of annual migration now explicitly prioritises "educated, higher-skilled and younger migrants", particularly those who are already studying or living in Australia.

Venture capital incentives are henceforth to favour "young, expanding firms". Twenty thousand small companies will be able to trouser refunds of fringe benefits and payroll tax, so long as they've been in operation for less than two years.

Tax breaks for electric vehicles, meanwhile, will be eased back gradually, because in the assessment of the budget's drafters, the electric vehicle industry is now "mature", and if there's a coda to this document, it's that if you're mature, you're probably ticking along OK.

Topic: Federal Government

Topic: Federal Government

Topic: Explainer

Analysis by Ian Verrender

The property and investment tax breaks aren't being turned off like a tap, of course. The changes are "prospective". New capital gains tax rules don't kick in until July next year. New tax arrangements for discretionary trusts come into effect a year after that — in July 2028 (by which time, presumably, if everything goes according to plan, Albanese will be riding toward election victory aboard a palanquin toted by young and muscular voters, while Angus Taylor or his replacement reedily vows to restore justice to tax minimisers, to an appreciative rattling of Zimmer frames).

We want to know what issues matter to this federal budget. Have your say.

Properties currently being negatively geared can still be negatively geared. This is thanks to the practice of "grandfathering" — a budgetary practice in which persons currently benefiting from a scheme are allowed to continue benefiting, in order to avoid mass panic and/or systems collapse.

"Grandfathering" is a term absolutely crying out for a rebranding, by the way. And not just because in the context of this "intergenerational justice" budget, it sounds a lot like making an exception for Grandpa and his 15 blocks of flats.

"Grandfathering" as a term dates back to the United States in the late 19th century, when various Southern states introduced new barriers to voter enrolment (literacy requirements, property requirements and so on). Voters whose grandfathers had been eligible to vote before the Civil War — and if you stop for a moment to consider what colour skin such citizens would universally have, the gambit becomes clear — were exempted from the new rules. So yeah, "grandfathering" does have rather an unfortunate historical connotation of the joke continuing, to some degree, to be on the disadvantaged.

Millennial and generation Z voters now constitute a majority of the electorate. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore )

But the biggest post-budget challenge facing Albanese: King of the Kids™ isn't going to be about the etymology of "grandfathering".

Albanese now faces the knottiest advocacy task of all: Convincing voters to accept a short- and mid-term hardship (the forfeiture of sweet tax breaks) in the interests of long-term fairness and prosperity.

The task is made more difficult by the fact that the Australian population is already deeply cheesed off. And by the fact that he literally just promised one year ago that he would absolutely not do the thing he's just done. AND by the fact that even the youthful beneficiaries of this ambitious redesign are not sitting quietly around radiograms, ears pricked for the good news of how the old guy in the Billy Bragg T-shirt has just taken up the cudgels on their behalf. Which is why we must all prepare for the days ahead, which will be full of Tim Wilson TikToks depicting Albanese as a Boomer who's filled his beak with tax breaks and publicly funded super, and now is pulling up the drawbridge behind him, breaking not only his solemn promise but also the hopes and dreams of teenage investors everywhere.

This is a test of advocacy, of persuasion and — indeed — of ambition. Also, of political identity.

For the Liberal Party, the encouragement of home ownership is a bone-deep value.

When Robert Menzies gathered the disparate anti-Labor forces together at Albury 82 years ago, preparatory to forming the Liberal Party, his evocation of Australia's "Forgotten People" was already laced rhetorically around the family home, which he deemed "the foundation of sanity and sobriety … the indispensable condition of continuity; its health determines the health of society as a whole".

Over his prime ministership, Menzies initiated cash handouts to first home buyers. Built houses. Encouraged the sale of public housing stock to tenants. Home ownership rates soared from 53 per cent to 77 per cent.

But just days ago, Albury voted for One Nation. So, either the Liberal Party isn't saying the right things on this issue, or it's saying them in the wrong language, or to the wrong people.

Which is why this particular moment, in Australia's history as a federation, is so extraordinarily a) challenging and b) interesting.
